newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's CSA sets sights on high-tech zone.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's CSA sets sights on high-tech zone.

text.p: If you build it, they will come.

That line from an American movie could apply to Malaysia's Multimedia Super Corridor (MSC), a high-technology, high-speed communications zone that has drawn commitments from 29 foreign and domestic information technology firms to set up shop there.
But for the investor trying to gain exposure to Malaysia's version of California's Silicon Valley, only a handful of publicly listed Malaysian firms have stepped forward.
"There are very, very few that actually have any concrete plans of being participants," said Laurence Lau, head of research at Thong & Kay Hian Research.
One such company is systems integrator Computer Systems Advisers (M) Bhd (CSA), which, along with 28 other firms, will break ground on a site in the zone this month.
CSA, which also designs software, sells information technology products and provides systems maintenance services, is the only pure high-technology Malaysian company so far in the MSC.
It joins a roster of well-known foreign names including Sun Microsystems Inc, NCR Corp, and Germany's Siemens.
Speaking in an interview, CSA managing director Chuah Tai Eu said the firm's recent listing and involvement in the MSC have brightened its prospects.
"The listing will help us to expand our business in a much faster pace," he said.
CSA, 45 percent owned by Singapore's CSA Holdings Ltd, made an initial public offering (IPO) in Malaysia on on April 28 of 5.99 million shares at 2.80 ringgit each.
CSA also made a rights issue of 5.88 million shares at 1.23 ringgit.

Gross proceeds from the rights and public issues totalled about 23.99 million ringgit ($9.6 million). The bulk of that -- 10 million ringgit -- will be used to acquire property for offices and warehouses for CSA's more than 500 employees and 22 branches.
Chuah said the IPO would also help reward and retain employees in a business that usually has high turnover.
Chuah said the MSC project "is one of the best environments in terms of the physical location".

The development will lie in a 14-by-50 km (nine-by-30 mile) zone extending south from Kuala Lumpur and linking the capital's new international airport and its future administrative capital of Putrajaya.

Malaysia's government hopes that within three years the corridor will provide such advanced services as smart schools, which will incorporate the Internet and other computer applications into their operations. Another idea is telemedicine, which uses high-tech communications to allow doctors to help each other from remote locations.
He said the infrastructure, financial incentives and other factors made the site attractive but would not give details of CSA's site in the zone.
"We will have some subsidiary, or our R&D (research and development) division there, or some joint venture to do some new thing," he said, without elaborating.

CSA, whose projects in Malaysia include a broker computer system linking the stock exchange's member firms and a port management information system in Kuching on Borneo island, reported net profit of 10.87 million ringgit last year.
Its turnover was 267.40 million, with information technology products sales contributing 35 to 40 percent. CSA sells computer products made by companies like Sun Micosystems and Compaq Computer Corp.
Customer-support services account for around 20-25 percent of revenues, with systems integration earning between 15 and 20 percent.
It has forecast net profit for this calendar year of 13.38 million ringgit. ($1=2.5 ringgit)
